title.en: The Utgard Contests: Drinking the Sea, Wrestling Old Age
title.zh: 烏特加德競賽：飲盡滄海、力戰暮年

region.en: Utgard, the giants' stronghold (symbolic pin at Jotunheimen, Norway)
region.zh: 巨人要塞烏特加德（象徵性定位於挪威尤通黑門山）

texts.period: Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230 (older mythic material); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, Codex Upsaliensis

source.work: Snorri, Gylfaginning chs. 44-47; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Thor, Loki and Thjalfi travel to the stronghold of Utgard-Loki and are set three contests. Thor must drain a drinking-horn (it is the sea, and he lowers it visibly), lift a grey cat (it is the Midgard-Serpent, and he raises one paw off the ground), and wrestle an old woman (she is Elli, Old Age itself, and he is forced to one knee). Thjalfi races a thought; Loki eats against fire itself. When the trickster-king reveals the illusions, he adds the cruelest doctrine of all: the giants had meant to kill them at the first tests - Skrymir's iron gloves were the mountain-range of the world, and the wrestling-match 'would never have been? ' - no man could stand before Old Age. The record is the Norse doctrine that strength has absolute rivals: the sea, the earth, and time.
summary.zh: 索爾、洛基與蒂亞爾菲前往烏特加德·洛基的要塞，被迫接受三項競賽。索爾須飲乾一隻號角（那是海洋，而他確實讓水位明顯下降），舉起一隻灰貓（那是環繞世界的大蛇，他抬起了它的一隻爪），並與一位老嫗角力（她是「暮年」本身，他只能單膝跪地）。蒂亞爾菲賽跑的對手是「思想」；洛基與火焰比賽吞食。當詭計之王揭穿幻象後，還補上一句最殘酷的教義：巨人們本想在第一輪就殺死他們——斯克利米爾的鐵手套原是世界的山脈，而那場角力「無人能敵」，因為無人能戰勝暮年。此記錄是北歐的教義：力量自有其絕對對手——海洋、大地與時間。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Gylfaginning's greatest adventure is a doctrine about the limits of strength, told as a tournament of illusions. Thor, Loki and the boy Thjalfi travel east into Jotunheim and spend a night in a vast hall - in the morning it is a glove: Skrymir's glove, the giant sleeping beside it. Skrymir travels with them, and his snoring, his stride and his food-sack test Thor three times on the road; each hammer-blow lands, and Skrymir only asks whether a leaf, an acorn or a bird has fallen on his head. At Utgard, the king sets the contests: Thjalfi races against Hugi (thought, unbeatable); Loki eats against Logi (fire, which consumes the trough, the bones and the table itself); and Thor must drink from a horn 'thought short by many' - and he drinks three deep draughts that lower the sea around the shore visibly; then lifts a cat off the ground with one paw - and the cat is Jormungand, arched, one foot raised; then wrestles the old nurse Elli - Old Age - and is brought to one knee.

The revelation is the myth's philosophy. Utgard-Loki confesses: 'I brought forth spells against you'; the horn was the sea; the cat was the Midgard-Serpent; Elli was Old Age, 'which no man can stand before, though he live to the world's end'. And the cruelest clause: 'I had purposed, had I known? ' - the text: 'had we known you were so mighty, you would never have come into the stronghold; for we had meant to destroy you with the first tests' - the giants' welcome was an execution, and the illusions were mercy. Then the giant offers to show Thor his match: two men who will fight him - 'and they were? ' - no one appears; the stronghold and its king vanish, 'and no castle and no king were to be seen'. Thor raises the hammer to strike and cannot find them; the record ends with the god swindled by geography.

The cultural functions are the doctrine of strength's absolute rivals and the theology of the borderline. In the Norse system, Thor's strength is the gods' insurance; the Utgard episode teaches what the insurance does not cover: the sea (drinkable only visibly), the earth's circumference (liftable only by a paw), and time (wrestled to one knee). It is a humility-doctrine delivered as comedy - the myth of a strongman beaten by the world's dimensions - and its politics are pointed: the giants' stronghold wins by wit and illusion, the same weapons Loki uses, so the frontier is shown as contestable by intelligence rather than muscle. And the wrestling-with-Old-Age is the myth-world's most precise existential statement: 'no man can stand before Old Age' - the sentence the whole Edda is written to prove.

For the atlas, the record anchors the impossible-contest family (the Greek labors' impossible tasks, the Chinese Sun Wukong's contests with Buddha's palm): each a hero tested by cosmic scale; the Norse one is unique in setting the tests against natural absolutes - sea, serpent, age - and in admitting defeat on the record.

functions: Doctrine of strength's absolute rivals: sea, serpent and Old Age
Humility-theology as comedy: the strongman beaten by the world's dimensions
Frontier politics: the giants win by illusion and intelligence, not muscle
Existential formula: no man can stand before Old Age

passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Gylfaginning ch. 46 (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Thor wrestled with the old nurse Elli, and was brought to one knee. The king revealed all: the horn was the sea, the cat the Midgard-Serpent, and Elli was Old Age, which no man can stand before, though he live to the world's end. The stronghold and its king then vanished, and no castle and no king were to be seen.

title.en: Idunn's Apples: The Gods' Youth and the Eagle's Bargain
title.zh: 伊登的蘋果：諸神的青春與巨鷹的交易

region.en: Asgard's orchard and Thjazi's eyrie (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 阿斯加德果園與夏茲之巢（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

texts.period: Haustlong (Thjodolfr of Hvinir, c. 900); Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Thjodolfr of Hvinir, Haustlong; Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 1-2; ed. Vigfusson & Powell, CPB 1883

texts.license: Public domain (CPB 1883; Brodeur 1916); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The gods' immortality is a produce-supply: Idunn the keeper keeps in her box the apples the gods bite when they feel age coming, and they grow young again. Loki, pressed by the eagle-shaped giant Thjazi, lures Idunn out of Asgard with a lie about apples better than hers - and the eagle carries her off. The gods age visibly; forced, Loki borrows Freyja's falcon-shape, flies to Thjazi's hall, turns Idunn into a nut and carries her back - pursued by the giant as an eagle; the Aesir set fire to the wood-shavings at the wall, and the burning eagle's wings drop him, and Thor kills him. The record is the aition of the gods' dependency on an orchard and the first dividend of the Skadi-feud: her father killed, she comes armed to Asgard.
summary.zh: 諸神的長生原來是一門農產品供應：看守者伊登在匣中保管那些蘋果，諸神感覺衰老將至時便咬上一口，重獲青春。洛基被化為巨鷹的巨人夏茲所迫，以謊言（外頭有更甜的蘋果）誘騙伊登離開阿斯加德——巨鷹遂將她擄走。諸神的容顏迅速衰老；被逼無奈，洛基借來芙蕾雅的游隼羽衣，飛至夏茲大廳，將伊登變作一顆核桃帶回——巨鷹窮追不捨；阿薩神族在牆邊點燃刨花，燒著鷹翼的巨人墜落，索爾隨即將其誅殺。此記錄既解釋了諸神對一座果園的依賴，也開啟了斯卡蒂世仇的序幕：父親被誅，她持械前來問罪。

texts.canonical_translation: Corpus Poeticum Boreale, ed. Vigfusson & Powell, Oxford 1883 (public domain); Skaldskaparmal via Brodeur 1916

narrative.en:
Skaldskaparmal opens its treasure-chapters with a myth of divine logistics. Idunn, wife of Bragi the skald-god, 'keeps in her box those apples which the gods shall bite of when they begin to grow old; and then they all become young again, and so it shall be even unto the day of Ragnarok'. The supply-chain's weakness is Loki: the giant Thjazi (in eagle-shape) catches him in the flesh-pot trick? - the episode: Odin, Hoenir and Loki cook an ox in the wood; the eagle demands his share; Loki strikes the eagle with the staff, and the staff sticks to the eagle and Loki to the staff, and the eagle flies off with him, offering release only on his oath: he must bring Idunn out of Asgard with her apples.

The abduction is engineered by a lie: Loki tells Idunn that he has found apples better than hers, and she should come and compare; out in the wood, Thjazi in eagle-shape snatches her and flies to Thrymheimr. The gods age visibly - 'their beards? ' - the prose: 'the gods began to grow old' at council, asking where Idunn was gone; Loki confesses under threat of death and borrows Freyja's falcon-shape. The rescue is the myth's flight-comedy: Loki flies to Thrymheimr, finds Idunn alone, turns her into a nut, carries her in his claws and flies home 'with all his might'; the eagle pursues; the Aesir, seeing the flight, gather wood-shavings at the wall and set fire to them; the falcon clears the wall; the eagle, wings alight, drops, and Thor kills him inside the enclosure.

The aftermath founds a dynasty of feud: Thjazi's daughter Skadi comes armed to Asgard to demand atonement, and gets it - a husband (Njord, by feet-choice) and her father's eyes set as stars. The skaldic evidence: Thjodolfr's Haustlong (c. 900), a shield-poem, narrates the whole episode in kennings - Idunn's box, the eagle's claws, the burning wings - centuries before Snorri, and Snorri retells it to gloss the poem.

Cultural functions: the doctrine that divine immortality is agricultural (the gods' youth depends on an orchard and a keeper); the negotiation-with-hostage grammar (the eagle's oath extracted from a captured trickster); and the shapeshifting-rescue (nut, falcon, eagle). In the atlas, the record anchors the rejuvenation-produce family (the Greek ambrosia, the Chinese peaches of immortality, the Inca coca of the gods? - the frame is fruit-of-life myths): each an immortality-crop guarded by a keeper; the Norse one is distinctive in being portable, in a box, in a woman's keeping, and stealable by oath.

functions: Aition of divine youth: the gods' immortality as an orchard-supply with a keeper
Hostage-oath grammar: the eagle's release price extracted from a captured trickster
Shapeshifting-rescue: nut, falcon and eagle in the flight home
Feud-origination: Skadi's armed arrival and her settlement found the Njord-marriage

title.en: Njord and Skadi: A Marriage of Sea and Mountain, Settled by Feet
title.zh: 尼奧德與斯卡蒂：以雙腳擇定的山海聯姻

region.en: Noatun by the sea and Thrymheim in the mountains (symbolic pin at Lofoten, Norway)
region.zh: 海邊的諾阿頓與山中的特呂姆海姆（象徵性定位於挪威羅弗敦）

texts.period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older material); Grimnismal st. 11, 15; principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to, GKS 2365 4to

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal ch. 3; Grimnismal st. 11, 15; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

texts.license: Public domain (Brodeur 1916; Bellows 1923); passages below are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: When the Aesir kill her father Thjazi, the giantess Skadi comes armed to Asgard for atonement. The settlement: she shall choose a husband from among the gods - by his feet. She picks the cleanest pair, believing them Baldr's; they are Njord's, and the marriage is made with the condition that each shall dwell nine nights in the other's home. The sea-hall deafens her with gulls; the mountain-hall wakes him with wolves; the compromise fails - and the myth of the failed divine marriage is also the aition of the shoreline's ecology: the place where sea-birds and wolves meet is the negotiated border between two households.
summary.zh: 阿薩神族誅殺其父夏茲後，女巨人斯卡蒂持械前來阿斯加德要求償付。和解條件是：她可從神族中自選一位丈夫——但只能看腳。她挑中雙足最潔淨者，以為是巴爾德，實則是尼奧德。婚約附加條款：夫妻須輪流在對方家中各住九夜。海邊大廳的海鳥鳴聲令她徹夜難眠；山中大廳的狼嚎又吵醒了海神。妥協失敗——而這則「失敗的神聖聯姻」神話，同時也是海岸線生態的起源故事：海鳥與狼群相遇之地，正是兩戶人家談判出的邊界。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The myth begins as a legal action. Skadi - 'the shining bride of the gods'? - the giantess, in helmet and byrnie and weapons of war, comes to Asgard to demand atonement for her father Thjazi, killed in the burning of the eagle. The Aesir offer compensation: she shall choose a husband from among them - 'but she shall choose by the feet only, and see nothing else of the man'. She finds one pair of feet passing fair and says: 'him I choose; little do I expect? ' - the text: 'there is little blemish, Baldr should be faultless in form' - and it is Njord of Noatun. The settlement also obliges the gods to make her laugh - Loki's trick (a goat's bait on his own beard, the rope tied to his testicles and to the goat's) does it - and to set her father's eyes as stars in the sky, which Odin does: 'the greatest memorials? ' - the two eyes thrown into the heaven as stars.

The marriage's terms are the myth's experimental clause: each shall dwell nine nights in the other's home. At Noatun, the sea-hall, the gulls' cries wake her: 'evil birds wake me that fly from the sea; every morning the gull wakes me'. At Thrymheim, the mountain-hall, the wolves' howls wake him: 'sick? ' - the prose: 'the wolves' howling wakes him, sick? ' - 'I was waked by the howling of wolves, he said? ' - the poem Grimnismal supplies the speeches in st. 11 and 15: each spouse testifies against the other's home. Neither can sleep in the other's world; the marriage dissolves by experiment, and Skadi returns to Thrymheim 'and abides there? ' - the text: 'she went up? ' - Snorri: 'Skadi then went up on the mountain and abode in Thrymheim, and often rides? ' - she keeps to the mountains, hunting on snowshoes with bow, and is called the snowshoe-goddess (ondurdís).

The record's cultural functions are the doctrine of habitat-marriage and the aition of the shore's ecology. The myth formalizes an observation about two landscapes - sea-shore and mountain - that cannot be inhabited by the other's household; the failed marriage is the boundary-negotiation of two ecological regimes, and the shoreline (where gull-cries and wolf-howls meet) is the myth's map of the compromise-point. And the feet-choice is the myth-world's theory of mate-selection: beauty is judged by its least poetic part, and the chooser guesses wrong - the doctrine that marriage by appearance mistakes its partner. Grimnismal's verse-argument (each spouse's testimony) is the poem's own trial-record, and Snorri's prose adds the judicial frame (atonement, choice, compensation, laugh-payment) that makes the whole episode read like a legal settlement of a feud.

In the atlas, the record anchors the divine-marriage family (Zeus-Hera's institution, the Izanagi-Izanami separation): each a marriage myth; the Norse one is distinctive in being failed by design - an experiment in cohabitation whose result is geography: the sea stays with the sea-folk, the mountain with the ski-goddess, and the boundary is the beach.

functions: Habitat-marriage doctrine: sea and mountain households cannot cohabit - the failed experiment maps the shoreline's ecology
Legal frame: the marriage as atonement, with feet-choice, laugh-payment and star-compensation
Mate-selection theory: beauty judged by feet, and the chooser guesses wrong
Skadi's office: the snowshoe-goddess of the mountains, bow and snowshoe as her cult-gear

title.en: Freyr of the Swedes: The God-King, Beli and the Mound at Uppsala
title.zh: 瑞典人的弗雷：神王、貝利與烏普薩拉的墳丘

region.en: Gamla Uppsala, Sweden (temple and royal mounds)
region.zh: 瑞典舊烏普薩拉（神廟與王家墳丘）

texts.period: Ynglinga saga c. 1225 (older material); Gylfaginning c. 1220-1230; Adam of Bremen, Gesta c. 1070s; principal MSS AM 41 4to, GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Ynglinga saga chs. 10-12; Gylfaginning ch. 37; Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis 4.26-27

texts.license: Public domain (Laing 1844; Brodeur 1916); Adam of Bremen passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Freyr, the Vanir hostage, becomes the first king of the Swedes and the god of their wealth: under his reign come the peace-froth? - the 'Frodi-peace'? - good seasons and peace. When he weds the giantess Gerd, he pledges his sword and later slays the giant Beli with a stag's antler, bare-handed. At his death his body is laid in a great mound at Uppsala, and the Swedes, still prospering, believe the god still alive beneath the barrow - offerings continue; the mound-cult of a buried god-king. Adam of Bremen, writing in the 1070s, saw the temple: Thor enthroned in the center, Wodan and Fricco (Freyr) with the enormous phallus on either side, sacrifices of nine males of every species hanging in the sacred grove. The record is the best-documented cult in the Norse corpus: god as king, king as buried god.
summary.zh: 華納人質弗雷成為瑞典人的開國之王，並成為其財富之神：其治下風調雨順、四海昇平。他娶巨人族女子葛德為妻時抵押了自己的寶劍，後來只能空手以鹿角誅殺巨人貝利。他死後，屍身被葬於烏普薩拉的巨大墳丘，而瑞典人見國運依舊昌隆，便相信神仍活在丘下——祭祀不絕。這是一座埋葬神王的墳丘崇拜。1070年代，不來梅的亞當親見其神廟：索爾居中而坐，沃坦與長著巨大陽具的弗里克科（弗雷）分列兩側，各種雄牲各九頭懸掛於神聖林中獻祭。此記錄是北歐文獻中記載最完備的崇拜：神即王，王即被葬之神。

texts.language: Old Norse / Old Icelandic; Latin (Adam of Bremen)
texts.canonical_translation: Samuel Laing, Heimskringla, London 1844 (public domain); Adam of Bremen via paraphrase per Tschan 1959

narrative.en:
The myth-histories fuse the god and the dynasty. In Ynglinga saga, Freyr (Frey) succeeds his father Njord as ruler of the Swedes and is called their king: 'in his days began the Fródi-peace' - good seasons and peace such that the Swedes attributed their wealth to him; he built a great temple at Uppsala and dedicated to himself? - the saga: he took up his dwelling at Uppsala 'and appointed? ' - the account continues that he established the great sacrifices there and the wealth of the Swedes was by his blessing. When he fell sick and died, his men buried him in a great mound 'in the Swedish manner'? - the text: 'and they laid him in a mound at Uppsala' - and because the good seasons continued, they believed he still lived beneath, and offerings were made to the mound 'as to a god': gold, rings and sacrifices poured into the barrow for three? years, until the Swedes understood he was dead - and then, the saga says, they burned him and worshipped him as a god still.

The prose Edda supplies the god's warrior-doctrine: Freyr, having pledged his sword for Gerd, meets the giant Beli and kills him bare-handed 'with a stag's horn' - Snorri's pointed economics: had Freyr kept his sword, 'then the giant would? ' - the text: 'the gods would be served by it at Ragnarok'; the god's martial poverty is the price of his marriage. Gylfaginning also names his gear: the ship Skidbladnir, folded like cloth in his purse, and the boar Gullinbursti with golden bristles that lights the dark.

The outsider's document fixes the cult's reality. Adam of Bremen, writing c. 1070s from the archbishopric's mission-station, describes the temple at Uppsala: 'the people? ' - the chronicle: a temple entirely of gold, in which three images stand - Thor, mightiest, enthroned in the center, with Wodan and Fricco on either side; Fricco (Freyr) is sculpted with an enormous phallus; the priests offer nine males of every species, male animals and men, and hang them in the sacred grove beside the temple; the grove's every tree is sacred, and a golden chain rings the temple's gable; sacrifices at nine-year intervals. The record is Europe's best-documented pagan cult-site, and its Fricco-phallus confirms the fertility-god's iconography that the sagas imply.

Cultural functions: the god-king doctrine (the deity as dynasty-founder, buried and worshipped in a mound - the mythic charter of Swedish sacral kingship); the naked-king economics (the fertility god fights without his sword because his marriage bought the harvest); and the mound-cult doctrine (offerings to a buried god whose prosperity proves his life - the mythic logic by which a barrow becomes a temple). In the atlas, the record anchors the god-king and mound-cult families (the Chinese sage-kings' temples, the Egyptian dead-god cults): each a ruler worshipped as god; the Norse one is distinctive in being a Vanir hostage whose marriage priced his arms.

functions: God-king doctrine: the deity as dynasty-founder, worshipped alive beneath the mound
Mound-cult charter: prosperity proves the buried god's life; offerings keep him fed
Naked-king economics: the fertility god fights bare-handed because his marriage bought the harvest
Outsider documentation: Adam of Bremen's temple description fixes the cult's reality

title.en: Freyja's Necklace: The Brisingamen, the Flea and the Duel
title.zh: 芙蕾雅的項鏈：布里辛嘉門、跳蚤與雙神決鬥

region.en: Folkvangr and the walls of Asgard (symbolic pin at Gamla Uppsala, Sweden)
region.zh: 弗爾克萬格與阿斯加德城牆（象徵性定位於瑞典舊烏普薩拉）

texts.period: Skaldskaparmal c. 1220-1230 (older material); Sörla tháttr (14th c.); principal MSS Codex Regius GKS 2367 4to

source.work: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal (the theft of Brisingamen); Sorla thattr in Flateyjarbok; critical ed. Faulkes (1987)

summary.en: The goddess Freyja owns the finest jewel of the gods, the necklace Brisingamen, bought from four dwarf-smiths at a night's price. Loki wants it: he turns himself into a flea, bites the sleeping goddess' cheek, and when she turns, steals the necklace from her neck. Heimdall, the watchman, sees him and pursues - both in seal-shape through the surf - and recovers it. The late Sörla þáttr variant darkens the doctrine: the necklace bought by promiscuity, a bargain with four dwarfs, and Odin's curse that she be war-stirred and never rest till a man is found to fight for it - the necklace as the engine of human war. The record is the aition of the gods' costliest possession and of watchman-theft: the finest object in Asgard is stolen by its own pest-control.
summary.zh: 女神芙蕾雅擁有諸神中最華美的寶物——布里辛嘉門項鏈，以一夜之價購自四位矮人工匠。洛基覬覦此物：他化作跳蚤，叮咬熟睡女神的臉頰；趁她翻身的瞬間，自其頸上偷走項鏈。守望者海姆達爾察覺並追擊——二神化作海豹穿越浪濤——終於奪回寶物。晚期《索爾拉短篇》將此教義染上陰影：項鏈以放縱為代價購得，是與四矮人的交易；奧丁更施以詛咒，令她為戰亂所擾、永無寧日，直到有人為此寶而戰——項鏈遂成為人間戰爭的引擎。此記錄解釋了諸神最昂貴財物的來歷，以及「守望者失竊」的主題：阿斯加德最珍貴之物，竟被自己的除蟲員偷走。

texts.canonical_translation: A. G. Brodeur, Snorri Sturluson: The Prose Edda, New York 1916 (public domain); Sorla thattr per paraphrase

narrative.en:
The necklace-episode is preserved in two registers. The skaldic-prose register (Skaldskaparmal's kenning-apparatus) documents the theft and the duel: Freyja wears the necklace Bris (Brisingamen, 'the necklace of the Brisings'); Loki covets it, tells no one, and changes himself into a flea; he creeps into her chamber where she sleeps with the necklace around her neck, bites her cheek so that she turns over, unclasps the necklace and takes it - and does not return it. Heimdall, the watchman, has seen him; he changes into seal-shape and pursues; Loki, seeing himself caught, changes into seal likewise, and the two fight in the surf; Heimdall wins and brings back the necklace. The kenning-doctrine: gold is 'Freyja's tears' and 'the necklace's? ' - the prose lists the necklace among the kenning-bases for gold, evidencing the myth's poetic currency.

The late prose variant (Sörla þáttr, in the 14th-c. Flateyjarbok) darkens the economics: the four dwarf-smiths make the necklace and refuse gold; Freyja pays the price each demands - a night apiece - and Odin, told of it, orders the necklace taken (Loki steals it as a flea again), and imposes the curse: she shall have the necklace again only if she brings two kings to war eternally, each fighting for it - 'and she stirred up war between kings, and they fought on? ' - the tháttr makes the necklace the engine of a war that only the Christian king Olaf Tryggvason's coming ends. The variant is a converted Icelander's moralization: the love-goddess's jewel re-narrated as the cause of human war, and the myth's oldest stratum (theft and duel) preserved inside a Christian parable.

The record's cultural functions are the economics of the gods' jewelry and the watchman-theft doctrine. Brisingamen is the myth-world's costliest object - bought at a price the goddess alone could pay - and its theft by the flea is the trickster's signature: the finest possession of the order is stolen through its own smallest gap. The duel of the two shapeshifters in seal-form is the myth's image of law-enforcement: the watchman who never sleeps recovers the treasure in the border-medium (sea) between worlds. And the late variant's war-engine doctrine documents the conversion-era moralization of the fertility-cult: love's necklace becomes war's cause, until a king of the new faith shuts the story.

In the atlas, the record anchors the divine-ornament-theft family (the Greek Ares' belt? - the girdle of Aphrodite; the Chinese He Shi-bi jade): each a prized object circulating through theft; the Norse one is distinctive in being won by a flea and adjudicated by a watchman in seal-shape.

functions: Economics of the gods' jewelry: the costliest object bought at a price only the goddess could pay
Watchman-theft doctrine: the finest possession stolen through its own smallest gap
Border-medium duel: law-enforcement in seal-shape through the surf
Conversion-era moralization: the necklace re-narrated as the engine of human war

passages.text: Loki changed himself into a flea, crept into Freyja's chamber, bit her cheek so that she turned, unclasped the necklace Brisingamen and took it away. Heimdall the watchman saw him, changed into seal-shape and pursued; Loki took seal-shape too, and they fought in the surf, and Heimdall won and brought back the necklace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Snorri, Skaldskaparmal (Brodeur 1916); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the late tale the necklace's price was paid to four dwarf-smiths, one night apiece; Odin ordered it stolen, and cursed Freyja: she should have it again only when two kings made war for it eternally - and she stirred up the war, until the coming of the new faith ended it.
